Long-run demand is perfectly inelastic because consumers have more time to adjust
Buyers are less sensitive to price changes when given more time to react.
Buyers necessarily have substantially more income after ten years.

questions.explanation: People have more time to change vehicles, travel habits or location, making long-run demand more elastic.

questions.stem: What does positive cross-price elasticity between two goods usually indicate?

options.text: Both must have perfectly inelastic demand

questions.explanation: A rise in one good’s price increases demand for the other when they are substitutes.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 29–30

questions.stem: Demand for printers falls when ink prices rise. What sign would the cross-price elasticity of printer demand with respect to ink price have?
questions.explanation: Complementary goods move in opposite directions for this cross-price relationship.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 29–30

questions.stem: A 10% income rise raises quantity demanded by 5%. What is income elasticity using those percentage changes?
questions.explanation: Income elasticity is 5/10 = 0.5; its positive sign indicates a normal good.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 34–35; new practice example

questions.stem: Quantity demanded falls as income rises, other things equal. What does the negative income elasticity indicate?

options.text: A substitute for every other good

questions.explanation: The income-elasticity sign distinguishes normal from inferior goods; inferior is not a quality judgement.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 34–35

questions.stem: A restaurant increases its pizza price from €12 to €15. Sales fall from 200 to 160 pizzas per week. Using initial values as the percentage-change base, what is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: Quantity change: (160 − 200)/200 = −20%. Price change: (15 − 12)/12 = 25%. PED = −20/25 = −0.8. Using the midpoint method instead gives −1.0; the method must be specified.

questions.stem: A drought reduces the available quantity of wheat by 20%. If PED is −0.5, use the percentage-change elasticity approximation to estimate the price increase needed for quantity demanded to fall by 20%.
questions.explanation: %ΔQ = PED × %ΔP, so %ΔP = −20%/−0.5 = 40%. This is the introductory approximation, not an exact large-change prediction from a constant-elasticity demand function.

questions.stem: Total expected extra marks from studying for 1–5 hours are 10, 14, 18, 21 and 23; total marks lost through tiredness are 0, 3, 7, 12 and 18. Which pair of durations ties for the highest net expected marks?
questions.explanation: Net benefits: 1 hour = 10 − 0 = 10; 2 = 14 − 3 = 11; 3 = 18 − 7 = 11; 4 = 21 − 12 = 9; 5 = 23 − 18 = 5. Both 2 and 3 hours maximise net marks. The third hour has MB = MC = 4, so it adds zero net benefit.

questions.stem: The price of bags rises from €11 to €13 and quantity demanded falls from 56 to 52. A further table row gives €15 and 44 bags. Using the initial point (€11, 56) and the €11 → €13 interval, what is the absolute price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: ΔQ = −4 and ΔP = 2. Initial-point estimate: (−4/2) × (11/56) = −0.392857, absolute value ≈ 0.39. The midpoint/arc value is about 0.44, which was incorrectly mixed into the original point-elasticity question.

questions.stem: Last year John bought 50 pounds of mincemeat when household income was €40,000. This year income was €30,000 and he bought 60 pounds. All else constant, his income elasticity is:

options.text: Negative, so mincemeat is an inferior good for John.
Positive, so mincemeat is a normal good for John.
Negative, so mincemeat is a normal good for John.
Positive, so mincemeat is an inferior good for John.

questions.explanation: Quantity rises as income falls. Using initial values gives (10/50)/(−10,000/40,000) = −0.8.

questions.stem: In any market where units sell at a common price, total revenue is price:

options.text: Divided by the price elasticity of demand
Multiplied by quantity minus production costs

questions.explanation: TR = P × Q. Subtracting costs gives profit.

questions.stem: The cross-price elasticity of food demand with respect to the price of entertainment is −0.7. If entertainment prices rise by 20%, the percentage-change approximation predicts that food quantity demanded:

options.text: Rises by 0.14%, and the goods are substitutes.
Falls by 14%, and the goods are complements.
Falls by 14%, and the goods are substitutes.
Falls by 0.14%, and the goods are complements.

questions.explanation: %ΔQfood = −0.7 × 20% = −14%. A negative cross-price elasticity identifies complements.

questions.stem: You and your housemate each eat three packets of Pot Noodles weekly. After your incomes rise, you buy more while your housemate buys fewer and substitutes preferred foods. Your income elasticity and your housemate’s are, respectively:
questions.explanation: The same product can be normal for one person and inferior for another.

chapters.title: Sellers — Production, Costs & Output Choice
chapters.description: Lectures 7–8 and seller slides: marginal products, costs, profits, revenue and supply response.

questions.stem: A firm has accounting profit of €30,000 and implicit opportunity costs of €40,000. What is its economic profit?
questions.explanation: Economic profit deducts implicit costs as well as financial costs.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 3; new practice example

questions.stem: Is it possible for accounting profit to be positive and economic profit to be negative?

options.text: No, accounting and economic profit are identical.
Yes, when total explicit and implicit opportunity costs exceed revenue even though explicit costs alone do not.
No, economic profit must always exceed accounting profit.
Yes, simply because fixed costs are a small proportion of total costs.

questions.explanation: Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs. Economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs.

questions.stem: In the production function A×f(K,L), what do K and L represent?
questions.explanation: The delivered production-function discussion identifies technology A, capital K and labour L.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 5; Lecture 8

questions.stem: What is marginal product?

options.text: The change in output from an additional unit of input
The total selling price of all units
The change in profit from altering price
The average fixed cost per worker

questions.explanation: Marginal product concerns incremental output from input, not marginal cost or revenue.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 7

questions.stem: Output rises from 80 to 95 when one more worker is added. What is that worker’s marginal product?
questions.explanation: The increment is 95−80 = 15 units.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 7; new practice example

questions.stem: If marginal product remains positive but is diminishing, what happens to total output?

options.text: It rises by progressively smaller increments
It rises by progressively larger increments

questions.explanation: Positive marginal product adds output; diminishing means the amount added is falling.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 6–7

questions.stem: What can cause diminishing marginal returns in the short run?

options.text: A guarantee that every input expands proportionately
The absence of any production limit
Bottlenecks as extra workers share fixed resources
A rule that every new worker has no skill

questions.explanation: The deck identifies bottlenecks and coordination costs as reasons additional workers contribute less.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 7

questions.stem: Which definition best captures the short run in cost analysis?

options.text: A period of exactly one calendar month
A period in which some inputs are fixed
A period in which revenue is necessarily zero
A period in which every input is freely variable

questions.explanation: The short/long-run distinction is about input adjustability, not one universal time length.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 8; Lecture 8

questions.stem: What distinguishes the long run?

options.text: Every firm must earn a positive profit

questions.explanation: The deck distinguishes long-run adjustment of both fixed and variable resources.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 8

questions.stem: Fixed cost is €200 and variable cost is €300 at output 100. What is total cost?
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 8–15; new practice example

questions.stem: At output 100 with total cost €500, what is average total cost?
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 9–15; new practice example

questions.stem: At output 100 with fixed cost €200, what is average fixed cost?
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 9–15; new practice example

questions.stem: As positive output rises, average fixed cost:
questions.explanation: AFC = FC/Q; an unchanged fixed cost is spread over more units.

questions.stem: Total cost rises from €500 to €560 when output rises from 100 to 120. What is average marginal cost over this batch?
questions.explanation: ΔTC/ΔQ = 60/20 = €3; the whole batch’s extra cost is not the per-unit cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 9–16; new practice example

questions.stem: If marginal cost is below average total cost, an increase in output causes average total cost to:
questions.explanation: Adding units that cost less than the current average lowers that average.

questions.stem: At what point does MC cross ATC in the standard smooth cost-curve diagram?
questions.explanation: MC below ATC lowers it and MC above ATC raises it, so the crossing identifies the minimum.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 17

questions.stem: In perfect competition, why is marginal revenue equal to price for an individual firm?

options.text: The firm is a price taker and can sell additional output at the market price
The firm chooses the market price

questions.explanation: A price-taking firm receives the same market price for an extra unit, so MR = P.

questions.stem: For a perfectly competitive firm that operates in the short run, an interior profit-maximising output on the rising part of MC satisfies:

options.text: Price = marginal cost = average total cost

questions.explanation: P = MR = MC is the output rule, provided operating covers variable costs. Equality with ATC is not required in the short run. The original four options omitted the general correct rule.

questions.stem: A firm has selected output using MR=MC, but price is below ATC there. What does this imply?

options.text: Revenue must be identical to producer surplus
The chosen output can still involve an economic loss

questions.explanation: Profit depends on total revenue relative to total cost, or P relative to ATC at that quantity.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 2, 4, 9–19; Lecture 8

questions.stem: What generally makes supply more price-elastic?

options.text: No inventory and no opportunity to alter production
A fixed capacity that cannot change
More adjustment time and easier access to extra productive resources

questions.explanation: Inventory, hiring flexibility and time increase responsiveness in the seller deck.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 22–23

questions.stem: A professional leaves a €120,000 salary to start a business. Which cost is most relevant to the economist but may not appear in the firm's accounts?
questions.explanation: The forgone salary is an implicit opportunity cost.

questions.stem: For an audit office, why might a partner's salary be treated differently as a fixed or variable cost?

options.text: Because the classification can depend on the time horizon and how the partner's workload changes with output
Because all salaries are always fixed
Because partner salaries are never costs
Because fixed costs always change with output

questions.explanation: Cost classification depends on the relevant time horizon and whether the expense varies with output.

questions.stem: A firm's total cost rises from €10,000 to €10,600 when output rises from 100 to 120 units. What is the marginal cost per additional unit?
At the current output, a firm's marginal revenue is €900 and marginal cost is €700. What should the firm do if it wants to increase profit?

options.text: Keep output unchanged because MR is irrelevant

questions.explanation: MR − MC = €900 − €700 = €200 for an additional unit, so expanding output can raise profit.

questions.stem: Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. Labour is the only variable input. What wage is paid per worker?
questions.explanation: VC/workers = €10/1 = €20/2 = €10 per worker.

questions.stem: Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. When which worker is employed do diminishing marginal returns begin?
questions.explanation: Marginal products for workers 1–8 are 25, 30, 31, 24, 20, 15, 10 and 5. The first decline is from 31 to 24 with the fourth worker.

questions.stem: Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. What is marginal cost per additional unit over the increase in output from 25 to 55 units?

Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. The firm is perfectly competitive, market price is €0.50 and fixed costs are unavoidable. Which pair of listed outputs maximises short-run profit?
questions.explanation: At 110: TR = 0.50 × 110 = €55; TC = 150 + 40 = €190; profit = −€135. At 130: TR = €65; TC = €200; profit = −€135. Net revenue TR − VC is €15 at both outputs; other table outputs yield less. Moving from 110 to 130 adds €10 revenue and €10 cost. Both maximise profit;

questions.stem: When land prices increase from €6,000 to €10,000 per acre but acreage supplied is unchanged, the price elasticity of supply over this change is:
questions.explanation: %ΔQs = 0, so PES = 0: perfectly inelastic supply over the observed range. The original stem asked for a property of supply but offered bare numbers.

questions.stem: According to marginal analysis, optimal decision-making involves:

options.text: Expanding an activity until total benefit is zero
Taking actions whenever marginal benefit is positive
Taking actions only if marginal cost is zero
Taking actions while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost; being indifferent to an increment when they are equal

questions.explanation: Compare additional benefit with additional cost. Equality adds zero net benefit and can produce tied optima.

chapters.title: Market Structure — Competition & Market Power
chapters.description: Verified Lecture 9 slides, including later slide-only sections; not a claim that all sections were delivered in class.

questions.stem: Which combination most closely describes perfect competition?

options.text: Many sellers, homogeneous products and free entry and exit
One supplier, a unique product and high entry barriers
Many differentiated sellers with strong individual price control
Few dominant firms with strategic interdependence

questions.explanation: These are the deck’s core perfect-competition characteristics.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 5

questions.stem: Assume a bakery is a price taker in a perfectly competitive bread market. Market demand slopes down; the bakery has fixed costs and rising marginal cost. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bakery can ensure that its price exceeds average cost.
The bakery faces a flat demand curve at the market price.
The bakery’s supply curve is horizontal.
The bakery always earns positive economic rent.

questions.explanation: The firm can sell at the given market price, so its own demand is horizontal. Merely having many bakeries would not establish price-taking without the added assumption.

questions.stem: What distinguishes an individual firm’s demand from market demand in perfect competition?

options.text: The firm’s curve has no price dimension
The firm’s curve is horizontal at market price even though market demand need not be
Market demand is determined by the firm’s fixed costs

questions.explanation: The slide’s perfectly elastic curve refers to the individual seller, not the entire market.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 6

questions.stem: Why can persistent profits attract entry in a competitive model?

options.text: Profits guarantee that market price will remain unchanged
New firms remove all customer demand
Entry is prohibited whenever profits rise
New firms seek profitable opportunities, increasing competitive pressure

questions.explanation: Free entry helps explain the long-run erosion of economic profit; short-run profits remain possible.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slides 5, 8

questions.stem: Which description best fits monopoly in the deck?

options.text: Many small differentiated sellers with free entry
Many suppliers selling identical products with no barriers
One supplier with substantial entry barriers and no close substitute for its product
Few firms whose choices always have no effect on rivals

questions.explanation: The monopoly characteristics contrast with competitive and oligopolistic structures.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 11

questions.stem: Why is a monopolist not free to sell unlimited output at any chosen price?

options.text: A monopoly always receives a legally fixed price
The demand relationship still constrains what buyers will purchase
Its marginal revenue is necessarily identical to price

questions.explanation: Market power means influence over price, not independence from demand.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slides 11, 16–17

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company holds a patent for a drug. What does the patent primarily represent in market-structure terms?

options.text: A legal barrier to entry that can create market power

questions.explanation: Patent protection restricts entry for the protected invention.

questions.stem: A water network has high fixed costs and low marginal costs, making one supplier cheaper than duplicated networks. Which concept describes this?
questions.explanation: One firm can serve the relevant market at lower total cost.

questions.stem: For inverse demand P = 100 − Q, what is total revenue?
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 17; label corrected

questions.stem: For inverse demand P = 100 − Q, what is marginal revenue in the continuous example?
questions.explanation: Differentiate TR=100Q−Q² with respect to Q; the slide’s MR line is incorrectly labelled P.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 17; label corrected

questions.stem: Why is MR below price for a single-price seller facing downward-sloping demand?

options.text: Selling more requires lowering the price, reducing revenue on units already sold
The seller pays no fixed costs
Buyers always pay more for the extra unit

questions.explanation: Additional revenue is reduced by the price cut applied to previous units.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 17

questions.stem: Which combination best fits monopolistic competition?

options.text: One seller with no close alternatives
A few firms protected by permanent entry barriers
Many sellers with exactly identical products and no pricing discretion
Many sellers, differentiated products and long-run entry and exit

questions.explanation: Differentiation distinguishes this structure from perfect competition.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slides 18–19

questions.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm earns positive economic profit and entry is easy. What is the likely long-run effect on its demand?

options.text: Demand shifts left as new firms enter.
Demand shifts right as competitors leave.

questions.explanation: Entrants compete for customers, reducing demand faced by each incumbent.

questions.stem: What does long-run zero economic profit mean for monopolistic competition in the deck?

options.text: Price equals average total cost at the chosen output
Every owner receives no normal return
Output must be at the minimum of ATC

questions.explanation: P=ATC removes economic profit but does not imply minimum ATC in this model.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slides 23–24

questions.stem: An oligopolist considers cutting its price. Which question matters most because of oligopolistic competition?

options.text: How are competitors likely to respond?
Will the firm become a price taker?

questions.explanation: A few large firms are strategically interdependent.

questions.stem: The largest firms have shares of 35%, 25%, 15% and 10%. What is CR3?
questions.explanation: CR3 adds the shares of the three largest firms: 35+25+15.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 28; new practice example

questions.stem: What does a concentration ratio measure?

options.text: The profit margin of the largest firm
The combined market share of a specified number of the largest firms
The sum of squared shares of every firm
The percentage of production costs that are fixed

questions.explanation: The deck defines CRn as summed shares, not the HHI measure asked in some past papers.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 28

questions.stem: In Porter’s framework, what can close substitutes do to industry profitability?

options.text: Make the threat of entry irrelevant in every case
Increase switching pressure and constrain pricing
Guarantee every incumbent unlimited pricing power

questions.explanation: The deck connects substitute availability with elasticity and competitive pressure.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 35

questions.stem: A firm depends on a unique input provider that can raise prices sharply. Which force is most direct?
questions.explanation: Supplier leverage arises from control of important inputs.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 37

questions.stem: What is the holdup risk associated with highly specific investments in a supplier relationship?

options.text: Asset specificity always prevents any contractual dispute
The supplier necessarily loses all bargaining power
Dependence can let the supplier demand better terms after investments are committed
Every investment is instantly reusable at full value elsewhere

questions.explanation: The GM/Fisher Body illustration connects specialised investment with vulnerability to supplier leverage.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 38

questions.stem: Which of the following markets can generally be considered competitive in the price-taking model?

options.text: Etsy, a platform where unique handcrafted products are offered for sale.
The market for tickets to a particular rock concert.

questions.explanation: Milk is the best approximation here to a standardised product with many suppliers; the alternatives involve differentiation, unique events or patent protection. This is a model approximation, not a claim that every milk market is perfectly competitive.

questions.stem: A monopolist faces P = 100 − Q and MR = 100 − 2Q. Marginal cost is constant at €20. What output maximises profit?
For the monopolist with P = 100 − Q, MR = 100 − 2Q and MC = €20, what price is charged at the profit-maximising output?
questions.explanation: Q = 40; substitute into demand: P = 100 − 40 = €60.

questions.stem: A monopolist sells 40 units at €60 each and has an average economic cost of €35 per unit. What is economic profit?
An accounting firm charges €1,200 per client, has average economic cost of €900 per client and serves 100 clients. What is economic profit?
A restaurant in monopolistic competition charges €40 per meal, has average economic cost of €50 and sells 500 meals. What is economic profit?
A restaurant’s reputation and distinctive dining experience allow it to charge €5 more than a similar competitor. What explains this pricing power?
questions.explanation: Customers perceive a difference and may prefer this restaurant.

questions.stem: In long-run monopolistic-competition equilibrium, a firm sells 2,000 units for €25 each and earns zero economic profit. What is average economic cost?
questions.explanation: Zero economic profit requires P = AC, so AC = €25.

questions.stem: Four firms have shares of 35%, 25%, 20% and 20%. What is the two-firm concentration ratio?
questions.explanation: Add the two largest shares: 35% + 25% = 60%.

questions.stem: Five firms have shares of 30%, 25%, 20%, 15% and 10%. What is the three-firm concentration ratio?
Two firms each have 45% of an industry; the remaining firms together have 10%. What is the two-firm concentration ratio?
An oligopolistic industry is profitable and has significant entry barriers. Which factor helps maintain profitability?

options.text: High entry barriers limiting competitive pressure

questions.explanation: Barriers restrict entry that might otherwise compete away economic profit.

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive firm faces P = €50. MC is €30 at Q = 40, €50 at Q = 50 and €70 at Q = 60. Assuming rising MC and that P covers AVC at Q = 50, what output should it choose?
questions.explanation: Choose Q = 50 where P = MC. The AVC assumption rules out shutdown.

questions.stem: A competitive firm produces 500 units at €40 each. MC is €25 and the next units also have MC below €40. What should it do?

options.text: Reduce output because price exceeds average cost.
Increase output because extra units cost less than the price received.
Keep output unchanged because MC is positive.
Stop producing because it is not a monopoly.

questions.explanation: Additional units add positive marginal profit while P = MR exceeds MC.

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive firm sells 1,000 units for €20 each. Average economic cost is €20. What is economic profit?
A commodity producer in perfect competition raises its price from €100 to €105 while identical products remain available for €100. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: It sells more because its price is higher.
It may sell none of its output.

questions.explanation: Buyers can purchase the identical product from rivals for less.

questions.stem: Why must an individual competitive firm’s demand curve be distinguished from the market demand curve?

options.text: A downward market demand curve means each small firm chooses the market price
The market demand curve is a cost curve
The firm takes the market price as given even though total market demand may slope downward

questions.explanation: A price-taking firm faces a horizontal demand curve at the given price; that is not the demand curve for the entire market.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 10, 13 October 2026 — notes and transcript

questions.stem: On standard smooth cost curves, marginal cost crosses average cost at the latter’s minimum. What explains this?

options.text: MC and AC measure exactly the same quantity at every output
The crossing occurs at maximum rather than minimum average cost
MC below AC lowers AC, while MC above AC raises AC
Any positive marginal cost must raise average cost

questions.explanation: The marginal-versus-average relationship explains the crossing at the minimum.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 10, 13 October 2026 — notes and transcript

questions.stem: A single-price monopolist faces P = 80 − 2Q. What is marginal revenue in the linear model used in the lecture?
questions.explanation: TR = (80 − 2Q)Q = 80Q − 2Q², giving marginal revenue with the same intercept and twice the negative slope.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 10, 13 October 2026 — notes and transcript

questions.stem: After finding monopoly output where MR equals MC, how is the selling price found?

options.text: Use the MR value as the selling price automatically
Read the price directly from the marginal-cost curve
Set price equal to average fixed cost at that output
Read the price from the demand curve at that output

questions.explanation: The demand curve gives willingness to pay at the chosen output; MR is not the price for a single-price monopolist.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 10, 13 October 2026 — notes and transcript

questions.stem: In the standard monopoly welfare comparison, why is a transfer from consumers to the producer not itself a deadweight loss?

options.text: A transfer changes who receives surplus; deadweight loss is surplus no longer realised
Every transfer destroys an equal amount of total surplus
Producer receipts are excluded from total surplus
Deadweight loss means only that a price has changed

questions.explanation: Redistribution and destruction of gains from trade are distinct effects.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 10, 13 October 2026 — notes and transcript

questions.stem: Which forgone trades create monopoly deadweight loss in the standard model?

options.text: Units consumers value above marginal cost but which are not sold because monopoly output is restricted
Units consumers value below production cost
Units where willingness to pay exactly covers no variable cost
Every unit exchanged in the competitive outcome

questions.explanation: Restricting output excludes otherwise mutually valuable trades, reducing total surplus.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 10, 13 October 2026 — notes and transcript

questions.stem: Which trade-off is relevant when discussing patents and market power?

options.text: Patents guarantee that no consumer can ever be harmed
Removing a patent always removes every barrier to entry
Temporary protection may encourage innovation but can also restrict competition and raise prices

questions.explanation: The lecture considers innovation incentives alongside monopoly welfare costs rather than treating market power as costless.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 10, 13 October 2026 — notes and transcript

questions.stem: In the standard long-run monopolistic-competition diagram, what does demand being tangent to average cost imply?

options.text: Marginal cost must equal minimum average cost
The firm produces at minimum average cost necessarily
Zero economic profit at the chosen output

questions.explanation: Tangency at the chosen output gives price equal to average economic cost, so economic profit is zero.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 10, 13 October 2026 — notes and transcript

questions.stem: Why does zero long-run economic profit in monopolistic competition not establish productive efficiency?

options.text: Zero profit means average cost is zero
The firm necessarily faces perfectly elastic demand
Zero profit makes every output equally efficient
The chosen output need not be at minimum average cost

questions.explanation: The standard tangency occurs to the left of minimum AC, so zero profit is distinct from producing at minimum average cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 10, 13 October 2026 — notes and transcript

questions.stem: At the standard long-run monopolistic-competition tangency with downward-sloping demand, how does price relate to marginal cost?

options.text: Price exceeds marginal cost even though economic profit is zero
Price equals marginal cost because profit is zero
Price must be below marginal cost

questions.explanation: MR = MC determines output, while demand gives P above MR; P = AC can still make economic profit zero.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 10, 13 October 2026 — notes and transcript

questions.stem: Several competing firms secretly agree to charge an artificially high common price rather than compete. Which concept best describes this agreement?
questions.explanation: The firms are agreeing to restrict price competition rather than setting prices independently.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 6, Lecture #11, 16 October 2026 — underlying transcript, oligopoly and collusion

questions.stem: In the simple oligopoly example, why would firms collectively prefer to coordinate price and output as though they were a single monopolist?

options.text: Coordinating as a monopolist forces each firm to charge marginal cost.
Coordination removes market demand as a constraint on sales.
A common high price automatically eliminates entry barriers.
Restricting competition can raise their combined profit compared with competing against one another.

questions.explanation: A cartel aims to obtain monopoly-like joint returns, although each member may still have an incentive to deviate.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 6, Lecture #11, 16 October 2026 — underlying transcript, oligopoly and collusion

questions.stem: Three firms agree to a high price. Suppose buyers see their products as identical and rivals initially keep the agreement. Why might one firm secretly cut its price slightly?

options.text: A lower price guarantees that its production cost falls by the same percentage.
It must lower its price to preserve exactly the same market share.
It may attract buyers away from the others and increase its own profit.
Undercutting makes the other firms legally obliged to stop selling.

questions.explanation: Individual gains from undercutting can conflict with the group’s interest in maintaining the agreed high price. The precise gain depends on demand and capacity.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 6, Lecture #11, 16 October 2026 — underlying transcript, oligopoly and collusion

questions.stem: Why can a price-fixing agreement unravel even when all participants would earn more if everyone kept it?

options.text: Joint profitability makes all participants indifferent to their own sales.
Each participant can have a private incentive to deviate from the agreement.
A high agreed price means buyers no longer compare prices.
Every agreement immediately converts differentiated products into identical ones.

questions.explanation: Collective benefit does not ensure that following the agreement is each firm’s best individual choice.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 6, Lecture #11, 16 October 2026 — underlying transcript, oligopoly and collusion

questions.stem: Why does involving more firms generally make a collusive agreement harder to sustain in the introductory lecture account?

options.text: There are more participants whose cooperation must be maintained and more opportunities for defection.
More firms necessarily give every participant the same production cost.
More participants remove every incentive to undercut the agreed price.
Each extra firm automatically increases the market’s total demand.

questions.explanation: Coordination is harder when more independently motivated participants must continue to cooperate; the lecture does not claim collusion always succeeds with few firms.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 6, Lecture #11, 16 October 2026 — underlying transcript, oligopoly and collusion

questions.stem: What does game theory study in the introductory oligopoly discussion?

options.text: How to calculate average cost without considering other firms.
How a price-taking firm accepts a price it cannot influence.
How to identify atomic values in a database table.
Strategic choices when each decision-maker’s outcome depends on what others do.

questions.explanation: Game theory addresses strategic interdependence. The lecture introduces the idea without requiring detailed equilibrium models.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 6, Lecture #11, 16 October 2026 — underlying transcript, oligopoly and collusion

questions.stem: A customer could buy a rival platform at the same price but would need to transfer data and learn unfamiliar software. Which barrier most directly explains reluctance to switch?

options.text: Economies of scale in the rival’s factory.
The seller’s fixed cost of entering the industry.
A legal monopoly created by a patent on every alternative.

questions.explanation: Switching costs include time, effort and disruption, not only an explicit monetary switching fee.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 6, Lecture #11, 16 October 2026 — underlying transcript, oligopoly and collusion

questions.stem: A new manufacturer can initially sell only a small volume, giving it a higher unit cost than established high-volume producers. Which entry barrier is illustrated?

options.text: Perfectly elastic demand facing every new manufacturer.
Economies of scale enjoyed by incumbents.
An absence of production costs for small firms.
A guarantee that all existing firms have identical products.

questions.explanation: Large-scale production can give incumbents a cost advantage that a small entrant cannot immediately match.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 6, Lecture #11, 16 October 2026 — underlying transcript, oligopoly and collusion

questions.stem: An investor can fund a new technology firm, but cannot readily recruit the specialist engineers needed to match established products. Which point does this illustrate?

options.text: Access to capital alone may not overcome scarce specialist expertise as an entry barrier.
Financial funding guarantees immediate access to every required skill.
A shortage of expertise means incumbents must be price takers.
Human expertise cannot affect a firm’s ability to enter a market.

questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes financial requirements from other entry barriers, including specialist talent and supply relationships.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 6, Lecture #11, 16 October 2026 — underlying transcript, oligopoly and collusion

questions.stem: Which statement about product characteristics is compatible with oligopoly?

options.text: Oligopoly requires every firm to sell a legally unique product.
Oligopoly requires identical products and no entry barriers.
Differentiation alone establishes that there is only one seller.
Products can be similar or differentiated; a few large firms and strategic interdependence are central.

questions.explanation: The lecture’s oligopoly discussion allows both similar and differentiated products. Product differentiation is not its sole defining feature.
